 C-Beauty, J-Beauty Win Shelf Space at Overseas Retailers
Cosmetics Exports From Both Countries Climb
 Finance | Published 2026.10.27. 06:30:05 | By Kim Yeon-ha yeona@sedaily.com | Summary | Save A A A ChatGPT Chinese and Japanese beauty brands are expanding into the U.S. and European markets as K-beauty's popularity lifts global interest in Asian cosmetics. Global beauty retailers are adding Chinese and Japanese labels after Korean ones, broadening their product lineups. Competition for shelf space among Korean, Chinese and Japanese brands is set to intensify in overseas distribution channels long dominated by K-beauty.
 A.S. Watson, the global health and beauty retailer, is stepping up support for Asian cosmetics brands through BrandLab, a brand incubation platform it recently launched, according to beauty industry sources on the 26th. The program covers C-beauty from China and J-beauty from Japan alongside K-beauty. That marks a shift in global retailers' Asian beauty strategy from a Korea-centered approach to one that includes China and Japan. Hong Kong-based A.S. Watson operates about 17,000 stores across 31 markets, including the British drugstore chain Superdrug and Kruidvat in the Netherlands and Belgium.
 Chinese cosmetics companies are rapidly building out their brick-and-mortar networks, led by the U.S. market. Proya, a Chinese cosmetics maker, is scheduled to enter 400 Ulta Beauty stores and the U.S. retail chain's online mall in November. Ulta Beauty has also been carrying Florasis, a Chinese color cosmetics brand, at some stores in the United Arab Emirates since last month. Global retailers are serving as the main sales gateway for Chinese brands going abroad.
 Ulta Beauty Chief Executive Kecia Steelman has also pointed to C-beauty's growth potential. Announcing second-quarter results in August, she said K-beauty sales rose by a double-digit percentage from a year earlier and stressed that C-beauty is also very important to the company. She added that the retailer would closely watch C-beauty and other global trends going forward.
 Chinese cosmetics brands are also gaining ground in Europe. Boots, the British drugstore chain, began carrying SHEGLAM, the beauty brand of Chinese fashion platform Shein, online and in stores in August last year. SHEGLAM also entered dm, a leading German drugstore chain, in October of the same year. Flower Knows, a Chinese color cosmetics brand, has likewise started reaching British consumers through Boots' beauty specialty stores.
 Expansion through upscale department stores and large retail chains is continuing as well. Florasis, which entered the Paris luxury department store La Samaritaine in 2024, plans to expand its distribution to U.S. retailers including Target and Nordstrom this year. Girlcult, another Chinese color cosmetics brand, entered the U.S. offline market by joining the flagship store of Asian beauty retailer Scorsh, which opened in New York in September last year. Chinese products now account for 15% of all beauty items Scorsh carries, triple the 5% share of two years ago.
 Japanese cosmetics companies are adding sales points in Europe and the United States. Curel, a Japanese skincare brand, entered pharmacies in Germany and France last year and this year expanded to five more European countries: the Netherlands, Sweden, Norway, Denmark and Finland. &honey, a Japanese hair care brand, sells its products through Ulta Beauty in the United States and Boots in Britain. Boots runs a dedicated J-beauty category on its official online mall, featuring Japanese brands such as Shiseido, Curel, Biore and &honey.
 Cosmetics exports from both countries are rising. China's cosmetics exports grew to $7.82 billion last year from $4.84 billion in 2021, according to the China Chamber of Commerce for Import and Export of Medicines and Health Products. Japan's cosmetics exports, which had been falling, also turned higher last year. Exports stood at 790.6 billion yen in 2021 before sliding to 515 billion yen in 2024, then rebounded to 572.8 billion yen last year, according to data from Japan's Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry.
 An industry official said global retailers that have seen K-beauty's success are widening their range to Chinese and Japanese brands to strengthen their product portfolios. "As retailers now have a wider choice of Asian beauty brands, competition to lock up major overseas sales channels will only get fiercer," the official said.
